In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of prostate cancer and its precursor lesions in the context of the prostate.
the development of new methods for the detection and treatment of prostate cancer.
the study of the relationship between prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels and the risk of prostate cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PSA testing is a valuable tool in prostate cancer detection.
the use of PSA screening in men aged between 50 and 74 years is associated with a 20% reduction in the risk of dying from prostate cancer.
men with a PSA of 4.0 ng/ml or greater and a single set of benign biopsy findings have an approximately 20% chance of harboring prostate cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PSA test has a low sensitivity for prostate cancer, but a high specificity.
the PSA test is a good screening test for prostate cancer.
men with a PSA level of 4 ng/ml and a negative biopsy have a low risk of prostate cancer and may be spared a second biopsy.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the risk for a second biopsy in men with an elevated PSA and one set of negative prostate biopsies is low, but the risk is higher for men with a PSA >10 ng/ml and for men with a history of a negative biopsy.
the risk for a positive biopsy is not the same for every man.
the majority of men with a single PSA of 4-10ng/mL who undergo a single negative biopsy are at very low risk for prostate cancer, even after accounting for PSA velocity.
